AARON ALDERMAN / DAD

Being here is part of the work.

On attention, boundaries, play and repair as Dad.

A personal essay · A working reflection, open to correction

I can be busy doing things for a child and still miss the person asking for my attention. The question I want to keep near is small enough to belong in an ordinary day: am I here with you, or only managing what happens next?

Being Dad gives care a particular responsibility. There is power in being the adult: the ability to decide, explain, protect, hurry, refuse. I want that power to help another person grow a life of their own. These are commitments I want to practise, with room to notice where my actions fall short.

IN THIS ESSAY

  1. Be here before solving it.
  2. Let protection make room for growth.
  3. Leave some of life unmeasured.
  4. Return after getting it wrong.
  5. Help a life become its own.

01

Be here before solving it.

There is a difference between hearing the outline of a difficulty and understanding what it is like for the person living it. I want to leave a little room between the first explanation I form and the answer I give.

That can mean putting something down, asking another question or letting a silence last. It can also mean joining what has caught a child’s attention without needing it to become useful. A shell, a drawing or a half-built thing can be worth our time before it becomes a lesson.

Attention is not a performance of endless availability. Work, tiredness and other responsibilities are real. I can be honest about a limit and make a promise I can keep: I cannot do this now; here is when I will come back. The return matters as much as the promise.

02

Let protection make room for growth.

A child’s growing will belongs in the relationship. I do not want agreement with me to become the measure of whether they are good, safe to love or worth hearing. Disagreement can be something we learn to handle together.

There are still boundaries to hold. Protecting someone, stopping harm and accepting the responsibility to decide can be part of care. The question is whether a boundary serves the person and the situation, or mainly protects my convenience, pride or need to be obeyed.

When I can offer a real choice, I want it to be real. When I cannot, I should say so without disguising an instruction as a question. Room to grow depends partly on knowing which choices are actually open.

03

Leave some of life unmeasured.

I do not want every shared hour to carry an improvement target. Play, wandering, making something peculiar and laughing at a joke that goes nowhere can belong to a good life without proving a result.

My interest in systems makes this a useful question to keep asking. A plan can help me remember what matters, but the plan should remain answerable to the people it is meant to serve. A child is not a project whose value appears in a progress report.

I want curiosity to have room to surprise both of us. Sometimes the better next step is to follow the question a little further instead of turning it into the answer I had prepared.

04

Return after getting it wrong.

The difficult test of care often arrives after an impatient answer or a promise I have failed to keep. I want repair to begin with what I actually did, rather than a long account of why I meant well.

An apology should not make a child responsible for making me feel better. I can name the action, hear its effect and say what I will try to change. Forgiveness cannot be demanded as proof that the apology worked.

Repair also needs something beyond a sentence. A kept commitment, a changed habit or a boundary that becomes clearer gives the words a place in what follows. I can return without pretending that the difficult moment never happened.

05

Help a life become its own.

I want to offer belonging that leaves room for difference: interests I do not share, questions I cannot answer and a future I cannot author on someone else’s behalf. Care can prepare a person to choose without trying to choose their whole life for them.

The same care needs to reach the wider household. My responsibilities sit among other people’s needs, limits and relationships. Being Dad is a particular role in that shared life, with a duty to listen beyond my own account of it.

The question I want to return to is practical: what would make my care more dependable here? Sometimes it is attention; sometimes a protective no; sometimes an apology; sometimes the simple pleasure of being together.

A question for an ordinary moment

Before deciding what to do, ask: what needs protection, what room can I give, and what promise can I actually keep?
